In short, with long-term contracts giving programme managers and departments only one lever to pull in order to change or create digital services, it’s never been more important that there is a choice within Government.

While there have been a few raised eyebrows at hiring in these straitened times, let me be clear that we need digital talent all across Government. Write a short blog post about replacing an old paper-based payments process with a digital service. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the post only.
final_message:
Every month, thousands of people across the country still put a cheque in an envelope, post it to a processing centre and wait. Then they wait some more. This is how one of our oldest payments processes has worked for decades, and it's time we retired it.

The paper process has a long history. A form is downloaded or requested by post, filled in by hand, and sent off with a cheque. At the other end, a team opens the envelope, keys the details into a system, checks them against another system, and banks the payment. If anything is missing or illegible, the whole bundle goes back in the post. A simple payment can take three weeks. A mistake can take three months.

None of this is anyone's fault. The process was designed when paper was the only option, and it has been patched ever since. But the cost is real. Users have no idea whether their payment arrived. Staff spend their days retyping information that someone has already written down once. And every error generates a phone call, which generates more paper.

So we started with the user, not the form. We sat with people as they paid, and with the staff who processed those payments. We learned that most users only needed to do three things: say who they are, say what they owe, and pay. Everything else on the form was there for the benefit of the back office, not the citizen.

The new service does those three things and no more. Users can pay by debit or credit card in a few minutes, on a phone if they prefer, and get a confirmation straight away. The details go directly into the case system, so nobody has to retype them. Staff who once opened envelopes now spend their time helping the small number of people who need a hand.

We released the first version to a small group of users within weeks, not years. It wasn't perfect. We found problems with the address lookup and with how we described one of the fees. We fixed them, released again and kept going. That's the point of building in the open and iterating: you learn from real users early, while changes are still cheap.

Early results are encouraging. Most payments now arrive on the day they are made. Errors have fallen sharply. Calls to the helpline have dropped too, which tells us people are finding what they need.

Let me be clear that going digital doesn't mean abandoning anyone. Paper will stay for those who need it, and we will keep supporting them. But it should be the exception, not the default.

What next? Other paper processes are waiting. If you run one, don't hesitate to get in touch. I'd like to help.
